tier_reason: First-party IBM/Eclipse write-up (openj9-website benchmark/daytrader3.md) against OpenJDK 9 HotSpot with CPU model, JDK builds and JVM options stated, but results are charts only, the run used a private OpenLiberty build with a beta ASM V6, and the JMeter/Db2 harness is not published, so it is not reproducible; vendor evidence stays C.

corrections.license: EPL-2.0 OR Apache-2.0 OR GPL-2.0-only WITH Classpath-exception-2.0 OR GPL-2.0-only WITH OpenJDK-assembly-exception-1.0
corrections.claimed_speedup: DayTrader 3 on OpenJDK 9: with AOT enabled (shared class cache populated by an earlier cold run) OpenJ9 startup is almost 40% lower than HotSpot, with AOT plus -Xquickstart almost 50% lower (page headline '2x faster startup'); with no options OpenJ9 starts slightly slower than HotSpot. Footprint about 60% less right after startup; during ramp-up HotSpot used about 80% more RSS (headline '40% less footprint'). Similar peak throughput, reached about 7 minutes sooner by OpenJ9. Single-core cloud test (AOT plus -Xtune:virtualized): headline '4x faster ramp up', HotSpot needs about 30 minutes to peak vs 7.5 minutes for default OpenJ9. Newer pages in the same repo: OpenJDK 11 DayTrader7 51-55% faster startup and 45-57% smaller startup footprint with SCC/AOT (benchmark/openjdk11-daytrader7.md); Quarkus REST+CRUD 64-66% faster startup, 18-37% smaller startup footprint (benchmark/quarkus.md).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: AdoptOpenJDK OpenJDK9-OPENJ9 build 20170925 (OpenJ9 VM 2.9, based on jdk-9+181) vs AdoptOpenJDK OpenJDK9 HotSpot build of the same date; OpenJ9 options -Xshareclasses -Xscmx60M -Xscmaxaot8M (AOT), plus -Xquickstart, and -Xscmx150M -Xscmaxaot120m -Xtune:virtualized (cloud tuning); -Xmx1g; long --add-modules/--add-exports list for both JVMs. Native build compiler not applicable.
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-3770K @ 3.50GHz, 16GB RAM, HyperThreading (8 hardware threads), CentOS 7.3; JVM pinned to 4 hardware threads; Db2 and JMeter on separate machines over 10Gb Ethernet (benchmark page). The OpenJDK 11 and Quarkus pages use the same i7-3770K.
corrections.caveats: First-party IBM/Eclipse benchmark on a 2012-era desktop CPU against OpenJDK 9 HotSpot (2017); results are shown only as charts and percentages. The startup and footprint wins depend on a shared class cache and AOT code populated by a previous cold run that is not counted; with no options OpenJ9 started slightly slower than HotSpot (OpenJDK 11 pages: similar without SCC). The run used a private OpenLiberty build with a beta ASM V6 library, so it cannot be reproduced exactly. Peak throughput is described as comparable, not faster. The repository README has no numbers. Newer eclipse.dev daytrader8 pages were not opened (blocked); figures for them are snippet only.

notes: All numbers in claimed_speedup appear on daytrader3.md; the record was accurate apart from the licence (four-way SPDX expression in LICENSE) and the missing caveat that default OpenJ9 starts slightly slower than HotSpot and the wins need a pre-populated shared class cache. Metadata checked: 3.5k stars, not archived, last commit 2026-10-05.

tier_reason: Upgraded C to A on the independent kostya/jit-benchmarks round 1 (2023-02-28): public benchmark code (BENCH/test.py per benchmark, docker/graalpython, docker/python3, docker/pypy3, run command 'graalpython --jvm' in tools/languages.rb), runtime versions (GraalPy 22.3.1, CPython 3.10.7, PyPy3 7.3.11) and CPU (AMD Ryzen 7 3800X) all stated, and it runs against CPython. The first-party docs/user/Performance.md 4x claim alone would be C (no hardware).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Independent kostya/jit-benchmarks round 1 (GraalPy 22.3.1 '--jvm' vs CPython 3.10.7, best time in s): binarytrees 2.02 vs 73.15, fannkuchredux 0.36 vs 4.04, fasta 3.53 vs 8.65, knucleotide 5.04 vs 8.41, mandelbrot 0.84 vs 37.52, matmul 1.4 vs 22.73, nbody 3.19 vs 53.72, spectralnorm 0.62 vs 20.69, brainfuck2 11.44 vs 142.26, brainfuck 14.22 vs >190 (CPython timed out); slower than CPython on pidigits 9.78 vs 6.17, regexdna 9.04 vs 5.2, revcomp 4.36 vs 2.45. Against PyPy3 7.3.11 GraalPy wins only 4 of 13 (binarytrees 2.02 vs 3.84, fannkuchredux 0.36 vs 0.71, nbody 3.19 vs 4.44, spectralnorm 0.62 vs 0.71) and loses 9 (e.g. brainfuck 14.22 vs 8.77, matmul 1.4 vs 0.36, mandelbrot 0.84 vs 0.54, regexdna 9.04 vs 2.38). First-party: GraalPy 25.1.3 geomean 4.30x faster than CPython 3.12.8 on pyperformance when JIT compiled (README '~4x', docs/user/assets/performance.svg); without the Graal JIT about 4x slower than CPython (docs/user/Performance.md).
corrections.baseline: CPython (first-party: CPython 3.12.8; independent suite: CPython 3.10.7); PyPy3 7.3.11 also in the independent suite, where GraalPy mostly loses
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Independent suite: GraalVM image with 'gu install python', run as 'graalpython --jvm <file>' (GraalPy 22.3.1, Python 3.8.5); CPython 3.10.7 from Ubuntu 22.10 apt; PyPy3 7.3.11 official linux64 tarball; Docker on Ubuntu 22.10. First-party: each interpreter installed via pyenv, 'pyperformance run', flags and JDK not stated.
corrections.hardware: Independent suite: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 80GB DDR4-3200, Docker on Ubuntu 22.10. First-party page states no hardware.
corrections.workload: Benchmarks Game style single-threaded programs (binarytrees, brainfuck, fannkuchredux, fasta, knucleotide, mandelbrot, matmul, nbody, pidigits, regexdna, revcomp, spectralnorm) run as whole processes in kostya/jit-benchmarks; first-party: pyperformance geomean over the pair-wise intersection of working benchmarks.
corrections.caveats: Java implementation (runs on the JVM or as a GraalVM native image), not a C++ library; listed because the claim is against Python implementations and its JIT is the Graal compiler. Independent numbers are for GraalPy 22.3.1 (Feb 2023), not the current release; whole-process times, so JVM startup and JIT warm-up are included. Against PyPy, the jits-category incumbent, GraalPy loses 9 of 13 benchmarks. Memory is far higher: 1.1-3.3 GB max RSS for GraalPy JVM vs 8-951 MB for CPython in the suite (binarytrees 3265 MB vs 98.5 MB). Without JIT compilation GraalPy is about 4x slower than CPython, so short scripts are slower; C-extension-heavy code benefits little. First-party 4x geomean has no hardware and only covers benchmarks that run on both.

notes: Upgraded C to A on kostya/jit-benchmarks (independent, reproducible, against CPython); the record's own caveat listed only 3 of GraalPy's 9 losses to PyPy, corrected. Shortcomings: slower than PyPy on most benchmarks, multi-GB memory, startup-dominated short runs slower than CPython, old version in the independent run, Java not C++. tier_reason: First-party gist (libriscv_bintr_vs_luajit.txt) with median/lowest/highest numbers against LuaJIT but no CPU, compiler, flags, LuaJIT version or linked harness code; the related rvscript repo has a BENCHMARK=1 build but the gist does not tie its numbers to it.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Gist, libriscv with libtcc binary translation vs LuaJIT, medians over 200x1200 samples with call overhead subtracted for both: call overhead 2 vs 156 ns; call args=8 7 vs 197 ns; syscall args=0 10 vs 174 ns; syscall string 13 vs 186 ns; complex syscall 50 vs 873 ns; integer math 6 vs 52 ns; array append 5 vs table append 18 ns; memcpy 18 vs 87 ns; memset 15 vs 67 ns; micro threads 102 vs coroutines 166 ns; sieve(10M) 80 vs 123 ms; fib(40) 66 vs 66 ns (equal); taylor(1K) 2234 vs 858 ns (LuaJIT about 2.6x faster, derived from page data). README: VM function call 3 ns vs ~50-150 ns for other solutions; libriscv can call a 3x-sinf function 5.25-7.25 times before wasmtime has called it once.
corrections.caveats: Gist does not state CPU, compiler flags, LuaJIT version or date (gist last active Oct 2025) and links no harness, so first-party tier C. The wins are mostly host-to-script call and syscall latency, which the author's rvscript README describes as the overhead of calling into Lua/LuaJIT from a game engine; it compares native-compiled RISC-V guest code against Lua scripts, not the same program. LuaJIT is about 2.6x faster on taylor(1K) (858 vs 2234 ns) and equal on fib(40); only sieve(10M) is a classic compute benchmark won (80 vs 123 ms). Benchmarks are hand-picked for game scripting; call overhead is subtracted from every result for both sides. Binary translation needs libtcc or an ahead-of-time translated build; the interpreted libriscv vs LuaJIT comparison is a separate gist. A sandbox/emulator with a JIT-like translator, not a drop-in replacement for LuaJIT as a language implementation.

notes: Numbers verified on the gist; the record omitted the taylor(1K) loss (LuaJIT 2.6x faster), now in claimed_speedup and caveats. Metadata checked: BSD-3-Clause, 1.1k stars, not archived or a fork, last commit 2026-09-30.
